headline_marked: [[npm install]] means trusting hundreds of strangers, creating a massive code-execution surface
headline: npm install means trusting hundreds of strangers, creating a massive code-execution surface
summary: Recent supply chain attacks like Shai-Hulud and Miasma have exploited npm's implicit trust in transitive dependencies, allowing malicious code to run with full user permissions on developer machines and build servers.
details: Most developers automatically run npm install, a routine that hides a critical security risk. This common practice grants execution rights to every package in your dependency tree, not just the ones you directly install.

In March 2026, the Axios library, used by 174,000 packages and downloaded 100 million times weekly, was compromised. Stolen credentials led to the injection of 'plain-crypto-js,' a malicious dependency that downloaded multi-stage payloads, including a remote access trojan.

This wasn't an isolated event. A September 2025 campaign hit 18 widely used packages like 'debug' and 'chalk,' which are woven into virtually all Node.js projects. With over 2.6 billion weekly downloads, attackers poisoned implicitly trusted components.

The Shai-Hulud campaign took this further with a self-propagation mechanism. Infected packages harvested npm tokens and GitHub credentials, then used them to publish poisoned versions of other packages maintained by the developer. This worm spread through the npm ecosystem's trust relationships, affecting 796 packages and 132 million monthly downloads.

The June 2026 Miasma attack introduced the 'Phantom Gyp' technique. A 157-byte 'binding.gyp' file in a compromised package triggers npm's automatic C/C++ compilation via node-gyp, bypassing the `--ignore-scripts` flag. This technique compromised 57 packages in two hours, targeting Red Hat's official namespace.
The core issue is structural: npm install executes code from all transitive dependencies, often dozens deep. An average npm project pulls in 79 transitive dependencies, many from unknown maintainers.

These packages' lifecycle scripts (preinstall, install, postinstall) run silently with full user permissions. On developer workstations, this means access to AWS credentials, SSH keys, GitHub tokens, and CI/CD secrets. Build servers often face even higher risks due to elevated access.

GitHub describes this as the 'single largest code-execution surface' in the npm ecosystem. This means attackers don't need to find a bug; they just need to inject code into a package, which is significantly easier.

Attackers primarily achieve this through account compromise, where a maintainer's credentials are stolen. This allows them to publish malicious versions of legitimate packages, exploiting the inherent trust.

headline_marked: [[AI compute costs 2.3x engineer payroll]] at Anthropic, far exceeding industry average
headline: AI compute costs 2.3x engineer payroll at Anthropic, far exceeding industry average
summary: Anthropic's compute spend is $515k per engineer annually, significantly higher than the top 1% of software companies at $89k, highlighting a structural shift in tech costs.
details: Anthropic's compute spend is 2.3 times its payroll, equating to $515,000 per engineer per year, against a $224,000 fully-loaded salary. This contrasts sharply with the top 1% of software companies, which spend $89,000 per engineer on AI annually. The median software company spends only $137.

With approximately 5,000 employees, Anthropic's inference and training spend is projected at $10 billion in 2026, translating to about $2 million in compute per employee per year. This indicates a structural cost base where infrastructure significantly outweighs payroll expenses.

The market faces three scenarios by 2029: Bear (token deflation wins), Base (top-1% trajectory tapers), and Bull (rest of market reaches Anthropic's ratio). Each scenario projects a different annual AI bill per engineer, illustrating potential future cost trajectories.

The Bull case suggests that the AI bill per engineer could match an entire median-SaaS employee's revenue contribution. Companies like Anthropic and OpenAI already generate $14 million and $6.5 million in revenue per employee, respectively, among the highest in the Forbes Global 2000.

Drivers for the Bull case include frontier model prices holding steady as training costs plateau and demand outstrips supply. Agentic workflows are also expected to dramatically increase token consumption, with Goldman Sachs forecasting a 24-fold rise by 2030.

Counterweights to rising costs include token prices, which have fallen tenfold per year for the last three years. Open-weight models are also closing the quality gap at a fraction of the cost, offering cheaper alternatives for companies.
